title: Fishing in a Landscape
fact: Joseon Korea, seventeenth century. Ink and light colour on silk. The seated fisherman wears a broad hat and a straw rain cape.
pair: That boat is easy to miss. Listen to the window rain, then look under the brim of the hat. Once you find the cape, that stretch of pale water has weather.
heading: Where did you look the second time?
aside: William James describes attention as a choice about what enters experience. Look once in silence and remember where your eye lands, then try with rain. You may quite reasonably look at the mountain both times.
gloss: My experience is what I agree to attend to.

title: Bowl with Fish and Waves in Relief
fact: Goryeo Korea, twelfth to thirteenth century. About 6.3 cm tall. The museum locates the fish and waves in shallow relief on the inside. Broad bowls like this held powdered tea.
pair: The photograph gives us a narrow ellipse at the rim and barely a glimpse of the fish. Over the sound of an ebbing tide, imagine drinking the tea. Which line would emerge first as the level fell?
heading: Finishing a work by using it
aside: Laozi draws attention to the empty part of a clay vessel. In this bowl that space does two things: it holds the tea, and as it empties it changes what the drinker can see.
gloss: Clay is shaped into a vessel; the empty space is what makes it useful.

title: Watching the Clouds Rise
fact: Ma Lin, Southern Song China, about 1256. The painting and Emperor Lizong’s calligraphy of a verse by Wang Wei once occupied opposite sides of a fan. The painting measures roughly 25 cm square.
pair: The piece is called Flowing Water. In the poem, the walker has reached the place where the water ends. I like the slight disagreement: the stream carries on in our ears while the man by the rock has already turned to watch the clouds.
heading: A verb that slows the eye
aside: Pause on the word ‘sit’. A fan does something a screen seldom does: to get from the writing to the painting you have to turn your wrist. That small pause in reading can give you back the time it took.
gloss: I walk to where the water ends, sit down, and watch the clouds rise.

title: Square Jar with Birds and Flowers
fact: Japan, Edo period, late seventeenth century. Hizen porcelain. The museum identifies different pairs of birds on the four faces, including cranes on one side and pheasants on another. This photograph offers one angle.
pair: The cranes are on this face; the pheasants wait around a corner. Try giving the jar a quarter turn in your mind whenever one of Debussy’s short piano phrases comes to rest.
heading: How much of a jar have you seen?
aside: Cover the near corner with a finger. For a moment the birds might be painted on a flat panel. Lift your finger and the corner folds the two designs apart again. That little experiment makes spatial perception quite tangible.

title: Laket with a Pin
fact: Central Congo, Kuba-style maker, early twentieth century. Raffia fibres form two alternating patterns. A metal pin roughly 24 cm long passes through the hat to secure it in the wearer’s hair.
pair: My eye followed the light and dark raffia around the dome before I noticed the pin had held a straight line all along. Follow the weave with the sitar, then let a beat on the tabla send your eye back along the pin.
heading: Putting the object back on a head
aside: Laket is the term recorded by the museum. Hide the pin and you might see a little basket. Bring it back into view and there is suddenly a place for a head and a knot of hair. The Indian recording is our present-day pairing.

title: Water Jar with Rainbird
fact: Zuni (A:shiwi) Pueblo, New Mexico, 1850–60. Zuni women used jars like this to collect, carry and store water. The museum cites potter Milford Nahohai’s suggestion that the curled beak may derive from the leading edge of a rain cloud.
pair: I saw the circle on the belly before I saw a beak. With the sound of rain, the line can curl into a cloud. The pot keeps the same mark throughout; the recording offers another way to see it.
heading: What else can that line become?
aside: Wittgenstein asked how a figure can stay exactly as it is while we suddenly see it differently. Find the bird, then try to find the cloud. The switch is yours to make. The suggestion about clouds comes from a Zuni potter.

title: Mountain Market, Clear with Rising Mist
fact: Joseon Korea, early sixteenth century. Ink on silk. The museum traces several encounters on the same scroll: a welcome in a courtyard, a greeting on a bridge and a walk along a cliff.
pair: When Greensleeves returns to its familiar tune, move to another bridge. How did the man we met in the courtyard get here? The scroll folds a day’s outing onto one surface, and the returning phrase is a way to find our bearings.
heading: The previous phrase is still with you
aside: Bergson uses melody to ask how an earlier note continues to shape the note we hear now. Try the same question here: if you had forgotten the welcome in the courtyard, would the encounter on the bridge still feel like a meeting of old friends?

title: Princes Hunting in a Rocky Landscape
fact: Mughal India, about 1580–85. Ink, light colour and gold on paper. In the pale drawing two lions have been encountered and one has attacked a hunter. The elaborate border was added around the eighteenth century.
pair: I turned the accompaniment down to a low wash of air. Without a drumbeat to announce the lion, you might enjoy the gilded border for a while before you notice a man is in danger. That delay is the reason for the quiet track.
heading: What did the border make you miss?
aside: Cover the border with two slips of paper and look again. A surround made more than a century later can still have the first say about where you look. Try naming the first figure you noticed each time.

title: Bowl with Flying Birds
fact: Iran, probably Kashan, 1280–1400. The museum identifies phoenixes and lotus blossoms and traces these motifs from Chinese decoration into Persian ceramics.
pair: It gets crowded inside this bowl. Pick out a white bird and a neighbouring blossom will lead you away. I chose a slowly shifting synthesizer chord to leave the beat open while you find your own way back to the bird.
heading: Look at the grey beside the bird
aside: A patch of grey that looked empty a second ago now holds the white outline in place. Looking can disclose that change immediately. To learn why the motif appears on an Iranian bowl, you need the history of objects in circulation.

title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
fact: Vincent van Gogh, 1889. Oil on canvas. The trees mass into a dark upright at the right; the bands of wheat and cloud run past them.
pair: In Debussy’s first Arabesque, groups of three meet groups of two. Listen for the notes that fall between the beats, then look at the field and sky. Both curl, yet no cloud traces the stalks directly beneath it.
heading: First a surge, then two rhythms
aside: Tap a steady beat with one hand. On a second hearing keep tapping and attend to the notes between taps. The dark tree can do something similar for the eye: it gives you a fixed point from which to notice the different directions of the brushstrokes.
